---

## Post 1 — hook  📎 fig1_before_after.png

Our RL pipeline produced an impossible result: plain supervised fine-tuning
beat PPO — at the exact thing PPO directly optimizes.

The cause was one default argument, three layers down.

A debugging war story, with the general lessons at the end. 🧵

> **Alt text**: Two-panel bar chart titled "One default argument made RL
> look broken." Left panel (retracted run): reward-model ranking accuracy at
> chance — 49.3% and 45.1% for the two reward models. Right panel (after the
> fix): both at 100% on train AND holdout. Caption: the only change was
> which side the tokenizer truncated from.

## Post 2 — why it's impossible

Why "SFT beats PPO" should set off alarms: PPO trains *against the same
reward model the eval uses*. It optimizing that score and losing to plain
imitation is your speedometer reading faster when you brake.

When a result is impossible, the pipeline is the hypothesis.

## Post 3 — the wrong hypothesis

First guess: the reward model is undertrained.

So: 5× the epochs, 2× the learning rate. Training loss moved by less than
0.002.

That's the tell. A "fix" that does literally NOTHING doesn't mean try
harder — it rules out the whole hypothesis class. Something structural is
wrong.

## Post 4 — the fingerprint

The clue we should have read first: the reward model's loss was stuck at
0.693.

Not "high". Not "noisy". Exactly ln(2) — the loss of a coin flip.

A Bradley–Terry model pinned at ln(2) is telling you it literally cannot
see any difference between the two answers it's comparing.

## Post 5 — the bug  📎 fig2_truncation.png

It couldn't see a difference because there wasn't one.

Contexts average ~1,010 tokens. The tokenizer truncates to 512 — from the
RIGHT, by default. The answer, the only part that differs between
"good" and "bad", was cut off entirely.

49 of 50 training pairs: byte-identical.

> **Alt text**: Diagram titled "The answer was truncated away before the
> model ever saw it." A long bar represents ~1,010 tokens of shared context
> followed by a short differing answer. A 512-token window anchored at the
> left (right-truncation) covers only shared context, so the chosen and
> rejected sequences become identical. A second window anchored at the right
> (left-truncation, the fix) keeps the answer.

## Post 6 — the fix

The fix is two lines: truncate from the LEFT (keep the answer, drop old
context) and widen the window 512 → 1024.

Reward model ranking accuracy: 49%/45% (coin flip) → 100% on train AND 100%
on held-out pairs, for both reward models.

## Post 7 — sanity restored

We retrained against the fixed reward models. The impossible inverted back
to sane:

base 68.6% < SFT 80.4% ≤ PPO (mean reward 2.22 vs SFT's 1.93) < Hodge-PPO
82.4% exploit resistance, n=51 held-out.

The "SFT beats PPO" result is retracted, not amended. It measured a bug.

## Post 8 — the honest number

About that Hodge-PPO 82.4% vs PPO 80.4%: at n=51 that's 42 vs 41 correct —
ONE example.

Directionally consistent with our embedding-level result (thread 1), and
NOT statistically significant. Both things are true; we're saying both.

## Post 9 — the bug's echo

Best part: our verification script reimplemented the formatting from
scratch — with the same right-truncation bug. It "audited" the fix and got
misleading numbers.

The tell, again, was an impossible inversion (lower train loss, worse
apparent holdout). Impossibilities are gifts.

## Post 10 — lessons + links (LONG)

The lessons we wrote on the wall:

1. Chance-level loss is a fingerprint, not noise. ln(2) means "inputs
   indistinguishable" — go look at the inputs.
2. A fix that changes nothing rules out its whole hypothesis class.
3. Anywhere long context + short answer meets a default truncation, the
   answer can silently vanish. Audit every truncation site.
4. Eval scripts must share the training code path, or they'll share its
   bugs — independently.

Everything (bug, fix, retraction, numbers): 
github.com/MikeHLee/shape_of_good_behavior
